newsitem.title: USA: Lugar says Clinton lets Weld drift in post battle.
newsitem.headline: Lugar says Clinton lets Weld drift in post battle.

text.p: Adding a new twist to a feud within the Republican Party, a key senator said Sunday he was unaware of any Clinton administration efforts to bolster the troubled nomination of William Weld as ambassador to Mexico.
"I'm not aware the administration is doing anything on behalf of Bill Weld," Senator Richard Lugar, an Indiana Republican, said on the NBC television programme "Meet the Press."

"And my guess is that this is a situation that has been sort of set out to drift," he said of the intra-party furore over Weld, a moderate Republican who resigned as Massachusetts governor to pursue the nomination.
Lugar has been increasingly outspoken in his criticism of Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, for refusing to hold a hearing on Weld's nomination.

He said administration action on behalf of Weld was "irrelevant to what ought to be done" -- by implication, the scheduling by Helms, a staunch conservative, of confirmation hearings, despite Helms's personal opposition to Weld.
"Advise and consent does not mean dictatorship. It means in essence we all participate," Lugar, the number two Republican on the Foreign Relations panel, said in renewing his challenge to Helms.

"He's a remarkable American senator and a patriot, but I do ask him to loosen up," Lugar went on. "We've really come to a point in the life of the Senate where we really have to have reciprocal relationships that are better."
Former top White House aide George Stephanopoulos agreed that Clinton ought to be doing more to help Weld.

"The White House has been exceptionally mealy mouthed on this nomination," Stephanopoulos said. "They say they're for Weld," but they rule out taking any steps to circumvent Helm's authority, he said.
"I don't think (Clinton) can afford to continue to put up nominees and then leave the impression that he's not fighting for them. I think that's the impression that's being left this week," he said.

Clinton nominated Weld last month, partly to build more bipartisanship in foreign policy. The nomination fight has exposed growing friction between moderate and conservative wings of the Republican Party.
Contending that Weld was soft on drugs, Helms has said he does not think he is qualified to be ambassador to Mexico, where curbing drug running is a key U.S. concern.
Weld, who has been mentioned as a possible candidate for the Republican presidential nomination in 2000, favours legalising marijuana for medicinal purposes and needle exchange programmes.
